clue.text: In which the scent assails the eye, not the nose

definitions.text: In which the scent assails the eye, not the nose

parts.words: In which the scent assails the eye, not the nose
parts.note: a hunt-like game whose trail is torn-up scraps followed by sight rather than smell

explanation.surface: A riddle about a hunt whose quarry is tracked by sight.
explanation.walkthrough: In this cross-country game the 'hares' scatter scraps of paper as the trail, so the 'scent' is seen rather than smelt.
explanation.definitionFit: A cross-country game in which runners follow a trail of scattered scraps, mimicking hounds on a scent.

clue.text: Everyone was expected to take it at 2

definitions.text: Everyone was expected to take it at 2

parts.words: Everyone was expected to take it at 2
parts.note: refers to the clue at 2-down, the ceremonial pipe passed round, from which each person draws once

explanation.surface: Something everyone had to take at two o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At 2' looks like a time; it is the pipe answered at 2-down, passed round so each person draws smoke from it.
explanation.definitionFit: A single draw of smoke from a pipe or cigarette.

clue.text: Presumably, navy-cut would be appropriate for it

definitions.text: Presumably, navy-cut would be appropriate for it

parts.words: Presumably, navy-cut would be appropriate for it
parts.note: Navy Cut was a brand of tobacco, and a cut navy suggests disarmament fitting a ceremony of reconciliation

explanation.surface: A remark on what tobacco suits which smoker.
explanation.walkthrough: Navy Cut was a well-known British tobacco; read literally, a navy cut back suits disarmament, so it fits the pipe smoked to seal a truce.
explanation.definitionFit: A ceremonial pipe smoked by Native American peoples to seal a treaty or truce.

clue.text: Subjects of a pictorial progress

parts.note: Hogarth's series of paintings A ... Progress traces a dissolute young heir's downfall

explanation.surface: The figures in a series of pictures.
explanation.walkthrough: Hogarth painted A Rake's Progress, eight scenes of a spendthrift's decline; the plural covers such profligates in general.
explanation.definitionFit: Dissolute pleasure-seeking men, like Hogarth's Tom Rakewell, are libertines.

clue.text: Snacks for the fire-side ?

parts.note: firedogs are iron supports in a hearth; a heated version would be a sausage snack

explanation.surface: Something to nibble by the hearth.
explanation.walkthrough: Firedogs (andirons) stand in the hearth beside the fire, where they get heated; the hot ones are sausages in a bun.
explanation.definitionFit: Sausages served in a long bread roll are a popular snack food.

clue.text: In the long run, they're usually conclusive

definitions.text: In the long run, they're usually conclusive

parts.words: In the long run, they're usually conclusive
parts.note: 'in the long run' means eventually, but here a long-distance race, which a final burst of speed decides

explanation.surface: A sage remark that things are decided eventually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the long run' sounds like 'eventually'; here it is a long-distance race, usually settled by a fast finish.
explanation.definitionFit: Short bursts of full speed, often at the end of a race, decide who wins.

clue.text: Only one on the dance floor?

definitions.text: Only one on the dance floor?

parts.words: Only one on the dance floor?
parts.note: reads like a lonely dancer, but means a single movement of the feet in a dance

explanation.surface: Someone dancing alone on an empty floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Only one' suggests a solitary person; it is one footfall, a single unit of a dance.
explanation.definitionFit: A dance is made up of individual foot movements, each one a separate pace or figure.

clue.text: Where shakers put it

parts.note: people shaking hands say the cheery phrase 'put it ...', meaning give me your hand

explanation.surface: A question about where cocktail shakers are stored.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakers sound like cocktail mixers or the religious sect; they are people shaking hands, who say 'Put it there!'
explanation.definitionFit: The handshake greeting 'Put it there' uses this adverb meaning in that place.

clue.text: The expert would seem to have had his day

definitions.text: The expert would seem to have had his day

parts.words: The expert would seem to have had his day
parts.note: a skilled practitioner's title read literally as a master whose time is gone

explanation.surface: A specialist who appears to be over the hill.
explanation.walkthrough: The title for a thorough expert, read word by word, suggests a master from the past.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone thoroughly skilled at an activity is an adept or virtuoso in it.

clue.text: Just the people to find insects under the vegetables

indicators.note: in a down clue the insects are placed beneath the vegetables

parts.note: peas are green vegetables
ants are insects

explanation.surface: Gardeners finding bugs beneath the crops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Under' places ANTS below PEAS in this down entry; 'Just the' and 'to find' merely join.
explanation.definitionFit: Agricultural labourers and small farmers, the rural common folk.

clue.text: Ensure free conveyance for an old European

explanation.surface: Arranging free travel for an elderly Continental.
explanation.walkthrough: To mark a letter so it travels post-free is to frank it; the Franks were an early Germanic people of Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: Stamping mail so the post carries it without further charge, and a member of the Germanic tribe that gave France its name.

clue.text: A short cape, succinctly described?

definitions.note: the definition names the quality of being so described, a noun for an adjectival phrase, hence the question mark

parts.note: terse means short or brief in expression
a ness is a headland or cape, as in Scottish place names

explanation.surface: A brief description of a small headland.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a cape described in few words; the answer is that very quality, built from a short word and a cape.
explanation.definitionFit: Brevity or conciseness of expression is the quality of speaking or writing succinctly.

clue.text: One likely to make quite a stir ?

definitions.text: One likely to make quite a stir ?

parts.words: One likely to make quite a stir ?
parts.note: sounds like a sensation-causing person, but describes a small utensil for stirring a cup

explanation.surface: A troublemaker who causes a commotion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make a stir' means cause a fuss; here it is literal, the stirring of tea in a cup.
explanation.definitionFit: A small spoon used to stir sugar or milk into a hot drink.

clue.text: Robert E. Lee's motive power

parts.note: the Robert E. Lee was a famous Mississippi paddle boat, driven by boilers rather than by the general

explanation.surface: What drove the Confederate general.
explanation.walkthrough: The general's name suggests his motives; the Robert E. Lee was the Mississippi steamboat that won a celebrated 1870 race.
explanation.definitionFit: Paddle boats on the Mississippi were driven by boiling water vapour from coal or wood-fired boilers.

clue.text: Like those of equal degree?

parts.note: degree suggests social rank, but means degrees of temperature, as on lines on a weather map

explanation.surface: People of matching social rank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of equal degree' sounds like social equals; it is equal temperature, as on lines joining such points on a map.
explanation.definitionFit: Having or marking the same temperature, as lines on a weather chart do.

clue.text: Hung by nine-and-twenty knights of fame in Branksome Hall

definitions.text: Hung by nine-and-twenty knights of fame in Branksome Hall

parts.words: Hung by nine-and-twenty knights of fame in Branksome Hall
parts.note: recalls Walter Scott's Lay of the Last Minstrel, where twenty-nine knights hang up their armour in the hall

explanation.surface: A line about knightly trophies in a Scottish castle.
explanation.walkthrough: Scott's poem The Lay of the Last Minstrel says 'Nine-and-twenty knights of fame / Hung their shields in Branksome Hall'.
explanation.definitionFit: Knights bore protective armour plates with their arms painted on, displayed on the walls of a hall.

clue.text: Incitement to frolic in the garden

definitions.note: the definition stands for a flower grown in such a place

indicators.note: the incitement is joined to the frolic, appended after it

parts.note: a lark is a frolic or prank
a spur is an incentive or incitement

explanation.surface: Encouraging some fun in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Incitement' reads as the start of the definition and 'in the garden' as scenery; the garden is the definition, and 'to' means the incitement is tacked on after the frolic.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall annual with spurred blue or purple blooms found in flower borders.

clue.text: River-man in the Wallace Collection

parts.note: the Wallace Collection is a London art gallery, but here it means the books of novelist Edgar Wallace

explanation.surface: A painting of a boatman hanging in a London gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: The Wallace Collection is a London museum of art; the clue means Edgar Wallace's novels, among them Sanders of the River, about a colonial commissioner.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgar Wallace's African stories centre on a district commissioner known from the title Sanders of the River.

clue.text: Bubbling with fun!

parts.note: the Latin root means boiling up, and the word now means overflowing with high spirits

explanation.surface: Someone full of high spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: The word comes from Latin for boiling up, so it can mean bubbling literally as well as exuberant.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheerful and full of energy, from the Latin for boiling over.

clue.text: Proposition from her to me

indicators.note: the answer is made from these words, their letters taken apart and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A suggestion passed from one person to another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From' signals that the answer is formed out of the letters of HERTOME, rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: In mathematics a statement to be proved is a proposition, a synonym.

clue.text: Mr. Wells's timely creation

parts.note: H. G. Wells wrote a novel about a device for travelling through the ages

explanation.surface: Praise for a well-timed invention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Timely' looks like 'well-timed'; it means 'of time': H. G. Wells's novel The Time Machine.
explanation.definitionFit: Wells's invention in his 1895 novel is a device for journeying through time.

clue.text: " This muddy — of decay " (Mer. of Venice)

definitions.text: " This muddy — of decay " (Mer. of Venice)

parts.words: " This muddy — of decay " (Mer. of Venice)
parts.note: a gap-fill from Lorenzo's speech in The Merchant of Venice, the missing word meaning the clothing of the body

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare quotation with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Lorenzo says that while 'this muddy vesture of decay' (the mortal body) encloses us, we cannot hear the music of the spheres.
explanation.definitionFit: The body is pictured as the garment of the soul, and the missing word is an old term for clothing or garb.

clue.text: Who said rum and veal don't mix ? They did in Herts

definitions.note: the definition stands for an old place in Hertfordshire

indicators.note: the letters of the two foods are mixed together, despite the clue's claim that they will not

explanation.surface: A dinner-party claim that rum and veal clash, rebutted by the locals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don't mix' denies what the anagram does: mix RUMVEAL. Verulam is the old name for St Albans in Hertfordshire (Herts), the Roman Verulamium.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman town of Verulamium survives as the name for St Albans' ancient site in the county.

clue.text: Seen at Court — in London

parts.note: noblemen attend the royal court

explanation.surface: People noticed at the royal court in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Peers of this rank appear at the royal court, and placed before 'Court' they name Earls Court, a district of west London.
explanation.definitionFit: Noblemen ranking above viscounts attend at the sovereign's court, and lend their name to the London district.

clue.text: Uncommon letter on show

parts.note: rare means uncommon
E is a letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: An unusual letter put on display.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the old 'raree show', a peep show carried round in a box.
explanation.definitionFit: A raree-show was a travelling peep show or street spectacle.

clue.text: Clams are possible ingredients for these sweets

indicators.note: the letters of the words named are the ingredients, which could possibly be mixed into the answer

explanation.surface: A recipe where shellfish might go into confectionery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possible ingredients for' tells you the letters of CLAMSARE can be rearranged into the sweets.
explanation.definitionFit: Chewy toffee-like confections made of boiled sugar, butter and milk are a kind of sweet.

clue.text: The glow-worm shows the — to be near" (Hamlet)

definitions.text: The glow-worm shows the — to be near" (Hamlet)

parts.words: The glow-worm shows the — to be near" (Hamlet)
parts.note: a gap-fill from the Ghost's farewell in Hamlet, the missing word meaning morning

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare quotation with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ghost in Hamlet leaves saying 'The glow-worm shows the matin to be near, / And gins to pale his uneffectual fire'.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for morning, the dawn that makes the glow-worm's light fade.

clue.text: Doubtless a person of vision

parts.note: a prophet sees the future and so has no doubts about it, a visionary in the literal sense

explanation.surface: A remark that someone is surely a visionary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Person of vision' is literal: a prophet who sees what is to come; 'doubtless' because such a person knows.
explanation.definitionFit: A prophet or soothsayer foresees the future, a visionary.

clue.text: One starts life in the pocket size

definitions.text: One starts life in the pocket size

parts.words: One starts life in the pocket size
parts.note: pocket-size suggests a small edition, but the creature is born tiny and grows in its mother's pouch

explanation.surface: Something that begins in a handy compact edition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pocket size' sounds like a small book; a kangaroo or koala is born minute and finishes growing in a pouch.
explanation.definitionFit: Kangaroos and their relatives carry their tiny newborn young in an abdominal pouch.

clue.text: Subject with which to open the meeting

indicators.note: the answer is the opening run of letters in the words that follow

explanation.surface: An agenda item to begin a gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With which to open' points to the opening five letters of 'the meeting'.
explanation.definitionFit: A topic under discussion is a subject, a synonym.

clue.text: They don't get drunk in shelters

explanation.surface: Abstainers who stay sober in their refuges.
explanation.walkthrough: The dregs at the bottom of a wine bottle are left undrunk; a lee is a place sheltered from the wind.
explanation.definitionFit: Sediment left in the bottle is not swallowed, and leeward places give protection from the weather.

clue.text: A group of stars attend church in Herefordshire

definitions.note: the definition stands for a town found in that English county

parts.note: Leo is the Lion constellation
a minster is a large or important church

explanation.surface: Celebrities going to a church service in the West Midlands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stars' suggests celebrities, but it is the constellation; 'attend' joins the two pieces. Herefordshire is an English county on the Welsh border.
explanation.definitionFit: A market town in the English county on the Welsh border.
